title: KiteWave Labs - Stitching throughput & savings console demo
summary: Intro demo of Redwood Optimize console focused on batching + prefix/KV cache recommendations and a cost model walkthrough for KiteWave's conversational search product. Discussed latency vs unit-cost tradeoffs, VPC/private deployment constraints, and pilot next steps.
action_items: Maya: Share sandbox link with cost-simulator and console perm so KiteWave can run 3 scenarios (low-latency, balanced, cost-first) - due 2027-07-23
Liam: Export model/throughput assumptions and example batching configs from today's run to GH gist - due 2027-07-22
Raj: Provide 7-day sample traffic histogram and top-10 prompt length distribution - due 2027-07-25
next_steps: Start 2-week pilot on Redwood Hosted with dedicated sandbox policy
Run the three cost-simulator scenarios and reconvene for results review (week of 2027-07-26)
Security review kickoff (Priya to send SOC2 and VPC onboarding checklist)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-20
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood CSM), Raj Patel (KiteWave CTO), Nina Gomez (ML Eng), Omar Hassan (Infra), Sasha Lee (Product)

0:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on this account, and Liam will do the technical run through. Priya's on for the security and onboarding bits.
0:08 Raj: Thanks, Maya. We appreciate it. We're trying to understand how Redwood's Optimize console can help reduce per-token cost for our conversational search while keeping P95 latency under 450ms.
0:15 Liam: Great, that's exactly what we'll focus on. I'll start by showing the baseline console run we imported — this is KiteWave's sample trace we were given. Note: some fields in the import got munged, so a couple of prompt names show as "query_ref_12" etc.
0:30 [screen share starts]
0:35 Liam: Okay, this is the Optimize dashboard — the Savings Simulator on the left. We imported your 7-day traffic, and the model profile is set to an Llama-style open model with 8k context, running in quantized fp16-ish path; the console picks kernels depending on seq dist.
0:50 Nina: Quick question — when you say quantized path, is that the 8-bit static quantize we ran in our POC or the newer Q4-2 profile?
0:58 Liam: The simulator used Q4_0 by default because the model artifacts you sent didn't include a quantization tag. That said, switching to Q4_2 increases single-token throughput but changes latency slightly; watch as I toggle it.
1:12 [click]
1:15 Liam: See that? Q4_2 lowers CPU-to-GPU transfer time in our sim and bumps batch throughput ~12% but adds ~8ms median latency in this simulated environment.
1:28 Raj: Hmm, 8ms seems fine if we get 12% more throughput. But our SLO is P95 < 450ms end-to-end — includes network and app time.
1:35 Maya: Right, and the console allows you to pick profiles by latency budget; we'll run three scenarios: low-latency, balanced, and cost-first. I'll spin those now.
1:44 [scenario run]
1:50 Liam: Scenario A (low-latency): we reduce batch sizes and prefer hot-path kernels, session affinity to avoid KV cache misses. Cost goes up ~38% in tokens cost but P95 drops from 320ms to 270ms in-sim.
2:10 Omar: Is that with prefix caching enabled? Our workload has a lot of repeated system prompts.
2:16 Liam: Good call — that sim disables prefix/KV prefetch. Scenario B (balanced): we enable prefix lookahead cache with a 30-second TTL and medium batch size. That yields ~18% cost savings versus baseline and P95 ~305ms.
2:32 Sasha: What's the hit rate assumption for that 30s TTL? Our search sessions last longer sometimes.
2:38 Liam: The sim uses a conservative 42% prefix hit-rate based on your sample trace; if your session affinity is higher and you pin users to shards, hit-rate can go above 60%.
2:50 Nina: How do we estimate hit-rate? Is it real-time from the console or we need to provide more telemetry?
2:56 Liam: Console can estimate from trace, but real production hit-rate depends on sessionization choices and cookie TTL. We gave you a small script we'll include in the sandbox to compute expected hit rate across sliding windows.
3:10 Maya: We linked the script in the shared doc — Console sandbox: https://redwood.internal/sandbox/kitewave-console-sim (note: internal link, will give access in the follow up).
3:22 Raj: Excellent. Can you walk through batching tradeoffs at different concurrencies? Our 200 RPS peak is bursty; we might see sustained 40-80 RPS but spikes to 200.
3:34 Liam: Sure — the console's concurrency slider simulates CPU/GPU saturation. For example, at 80 concurrent inflight requests, batching increases effective tokens/sec but raises tail latency. There's a recommended concurrency cap for each GPU profile.
3:49 [visual: concurrency vs cost chart]
3:55 Liam: If you use dynamic batching with a 50ms batch window, you get 20% unit cost reduction for chat-style prompts with avg length 120 tokens, but P95 climbs by ~30ms.
4:11 Omar: About KV cache — can you clarify differences between prefix cache and session KV? We run multiple short conversations for the same user in parallel.
4:20 Liam: Prefix cache stores identical initial prompt prefixes (system + instructions) and can be shared across users; session KV stores per-session KV cache (the model activations) which is sticky to the session. Prefetch (lookahead) will warm prefix entries based on user navigation patterns to increase hit-rate.
4:37 Nina: Is the session KV persisted across model restarts if we're on Redwood Dedicated?
4:41 Liam: If you run on Redwood Dedicated or Private with persistent worker pools, yes — KV can be retained across a pod's lifetime. On Hosted there's eviction policies, but you can request pinned session pools for pilots.
4:55 Raj: Security: we need to know how keys and logs are handled. KMS integration is required, and we need audit logs forwarded.
5:02 Priya: We'll send the KMS/HSM integration guide. Redwood supports customer-managed keys and can forward audit logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3. Note: SOC2 artifacts will be in the security packet.
5:14 Raj: Do you support bringing your own VPC or do we need to use a transit?
5:18 Maya: For Private deployments, you can bring a VPC or use a peered network connection. For Hosted pilot we usually do a secure tunnel and data plane isolation. Priya will follow up with the onboarding checklist.
5:28 [notes: security doc link - redwood.com/security/kitewave-pack.pdf]
5:34 Liam: Back to cost: here's the Cost Breakdown view. Tokens, model compute, network, and cache lookup ops are separated. For your workload, cache lookup ops are cheap relative to token cost but they add a small CPU overhead if you have high lookup RPS.
5:51 Nina: Could lookups create a hot-key problem? We have a handful of very popular prefixes.
5:56 Liam: Yes — recommended to shard prefix keys by user shard or add randomized key suffix to spread. Console's routing policy can route hot keys to dedicated worker pools to avoid contention.
6:10 Raj: If we shift to more prefetch and KV caching, what changes in our per-month bill? Give a concrete example with our baseline 3M monthly tokens.
6:19 Liam: In the Balanced scenario we showed, 3M tokens baseline cost of $12,000 would drop to ~$9,800 after ~18% savings. If you tune for cost-first (aggressive prefetch + larger batches + quantize Q4_2) you could go down to ~$7,400 but P95 will rise and quality regressions must be validated.
6:38 Sasha: Quality regressions — have you had customers notice hallucination or truncation after quantize?
6:44 Liam: Some edge cases — quantization can change numeric precision and rare token logits; this is why Redwood Optimize ties evaluations to prompt sets so we can flag regressions. We strongly recommend a small A/B roll out and running your regen prompts through the test harness.
6:58 Maya: We'll include a baseline eval set in the sandbox and show the console's quality drift alerts.
7:06 [screen: evals tab showing a few flagged prompts]
7:12 Nina: Nice, that should help. One more technical — does the console support hybrid routing? e.g., route high priority traffic to Dedicated and overflow to Hosted?
7:20 Liam: Yes, routing policies support tiered models and fallbacks. You can pin critical routes to Dedicated and set overflow to the cheaper hosted variants; console will simulate fallback cost and latency.
7:32 Raj: Timeline question — if we start a 2-week pilot, how soon can we see savings data?
7:37 Maya: You should get simulated projections immediately. For real traffic pilot, after 48–72 hours we can produce initial hit-rate and savings trends.
7:45 Omar: On infra: if we need session affinity to improve KV hit-rate, we might need sticky LB rules in front of your workers. Do you handle that?
7:53 Liam: For Hosted pilot we provide session-affinity tokens; for Private/Dedicated you control the LB but Redwood has an ingress spec we give you.
8:02 [pause]
8:06 Raj: Can you remind me of the fallback behavior if a model variant isn't available? We don't want user-facing errors.
8:12 Liam: Console config lets you set automatic fallback to a compatible model (usually a slightly smaller variant) or route to a 'degraded' path that serves cached completions for certain query types. You can also define soft-SLOs to drop non-critical features.
8:24 Sasha: Any compliance red flags for us? We are occasionally dealing with PHI in transcripts.
8:29 Priya: For PHI, Private deployment is recommended. We support customer-managed keys, private networking, and audit log retention policies to meet HIPAA-like requirements; we'll surface legal templates but your legal team should validate.
8:42 Nina: Small nit — some of the console terminology in the simulator reads "K V cash" in the legend. It's annoying when transcription puts spaces.
8:49 Liam: Yep we've seen that; localization of labels is on our backlog.
8:53 [laughter]
8:55 Maya: Ok switching to the savings detail sheet. This is the shared simulation export — I'll walk through the numbers.
9:03 [sheet displayed]
9:06 Maya: Column A is scenario name, B is assumed prefix hit-rate, C is batch window, D concurrency cap, E token cost, F net monthly cost, G delta vs baseline. For your baseline, we imported 3M tokens/month and a median prompt length of 98 tokens.
9:24 Raj: Where does network egress sit in that sheet? Our architecture pays a lot for cross-region egress.
9:30 Liam: Network egress is shown as a separate line item; if you run in-region Dedicated or Private, egress drops significantly. We'll annotate that in the exported CSV.
9:40 Nina: Can we run the cost model with different sessionization TTLs? 30s vs 5m?
9:46 Liam: Yep — the simulator supports TTL sweeps. Increasing TTL raises hit-rate but also increases memory usage; we show required memory footprint per worker so you can size pools.
9:57 Omar: Memory footprint numbers — are those for the model KV only or include prefix cache indexing?
10:02 Liam: Both. We break out persistent KV size and prefix index size. The console will show expected RAM per GPU and recommend worker counts.
10:12 Raj: Hypothetical: if we aim for cost-first and accept P95 of 520ms, what's required infra?
10:20 Liam: You'd need larger batch windows, higher concurrency, and a higher hit-rate ~60%. That drives memory pressure so you'd increase worker count and perhaps use Dedicated with pinned pools to avoid cold starts. The console shows the monthly amortized worker cost in the sheet.
10:36 Maya: I also want to highlight the rollout pattern: start with a tiny canary, monitor quality alerts in the console, then ramp using A/B and automatic fallback to previous variant if quality drops.
10:47 Sasha: Who owns the fallback circuit? Is it automatic or do we have to flip it?
10:51 Liam: It's configurable — you can set thresholds for automatic fallback, or we can link it to an ops webhook and let your platform decide.
10:59 [screen note: webhook config dialog]
11:03 Raj: On contractual terms — how do pilot pricing and credits work?
11:08 Maya: For pilots we give sandbox credits and a reduced pilot rate; if you commit to Dedicated within 60 days we can apply pilot spend to the initial month. I'll include pricing scenarios in the follow up.
11:18 Raj: Great. There's a potential integration with our realtime search cache that could reduce prompt length by pre-resolving entities — if we do that, does it change the calculations?
11:28 Liam: Yes — reducing prompt length directly reduces token cost and increases chance of packing more items per batch. We can model that in the simulator; bring an example prompt and we can prepare a 'shortened prompt' sim.
11:40 Nina: For the quality drift tests, what metrics are used? Rouge? BLEU? We use a custom relevance metric.
11:47 Liam: Console integrates arbitrary eval metrics — you can upload CSVs of your relevance scores and the sim will show drift relative to baseline using your metric. We also compute token-level divergence heuristics.
11:58 Raj: Ok that's useful. Anything else on the tech side before we wrap?
12:03 Sasha: One more on ops — if we route hot keys to a dedicated pool, can that be autoscaled?
12:09 Liam: Dedicated pools can autoscale but scaling rules are different — we recommend slightly more conservative thresholds for hot-key pools to avoid thrash.
12:18 Maya: Quick recap and next steps then.
12:21 Maya: 1) We'll share sandbox access and cost-simulator. 2) Liam will post the batching configs and example gist. 3) Raj will provide traffic histogram. 4) Priya will send security packet and onboarding checklist. 5) Schedule follow-up for results review week of 2027-07-26.
12:39 Raj: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
12:42 Nina: Thanks, this was super actionable.
12:45 Maya: Great, we'll follow up via email with links and dates.
12:49 [call ends]

Notes: transcript contains occasional ASR errors (KV shown as K V, "sock two" transcription for SOC2 in some exports), speaker labels are as recorded.
